senses: A type of still life painting, symbolic of mortality, characteristic of Dutch painting of the 16th and 17th centuries.
ety: From Latin vānitās. Doublet of vanity.
examples: In her straight-ahead photographs of storefronts, an arrangement of shoes or shrink-wrapped furniture becomes a vanitas still life.

senses: The fruit of this tree; the pulp is used as spice in Asian cooking and in Worcestershire sauce.
Diploglottis australis, native tamarind, a rainforest tree of Eastern Australia.
Garcinia gummi-gutta, Malabar tamarind, native to Indonesia.
A velvet tamarind (Dialium spp.).
A dark brown color, like that of tamarind pulp (also called tamarind brown).
ety: From Late Middle English thamarynde, from Old French tamarinde, from Medieval Latin tamarindus, from Arabic تَمْر هِنْدِيّ (tamr hindiyy, literally “Indian date”).
examples: Currently, the Palestinian territories are being featured, and the menu boasts treats like maftoul (a garlicky chicken and couscous dish) and tamar Hindi (chilled tamarind juice with rose water).
He began to crack tamarinds, pulling out the pod flesh, adding sugar and black pepper from his palms.

senses: The flavoured tobacco used in paan.
A sweet South Asian dish of boiled rice with milk, sugar and spices.
ety: Hindi ज़र्दा (zardā); Urdu زردہ.
examples: Hookah samples collected from urban “hookah bars” from Bengaluru were found to contain nicotine content of 0.8 mg/g, while, in zarda, average nicotine was 20.35 mg/g.

senses: A flat disc of metal or stone thrown at a target in the game of quoits.
A ring of rubber or rope similarly used in the game of deck-quoits.
The flat stone covering a cromlech.
An ancient burial mound, synonymous with dolmen.
The discus used in ancient sports.
ety: From Middle English coyte (“flat stone”), from Old French coite, from Latin culcita. Doublet of quilt.
examples: He heard then a warm heavy sigh, softer, as she turned over and the loose brass quoits of the bedstead jingled. Must get those settled really.
This quoit was brought from a karn about a furlong distance, near which is another cromlech, not so large.

senses: The individual act or recurring practice of stealing items of low value, especially in small quantities, for which the legal term is petty theft.
ety: From pilfer + -age.
examples: Still, there is pilferage, mysterious discrepancies eating into the percentages.

senses: A money laundering operation.
ety: Blend of laundry + automatic. From Laundromat, (former) trademark (1940s) of Westinghouse Electric Corporation for its washing machines, coined by Westinghouse publicist George Edward Pendray.
examples: The Russian laundromat was soon nicknamed the Moldovan laundromat, as it centred on transactions between Russia and the small, poor country locked between Ukraine and Romania.

senses: To defeat in terms of firepower.
ety: From out- + gun.
examples: There is no sporting purpose on earth that should stop the United States Congress from banishing assault weapons that outgun police and cut down children.

senses: The act of ascertaining.
ety: From ascertain + -ment.
examples: The ascertainment of death takes place in the chapel, rather than in the room where he died, and his body is immediately placed inside the coffin.

senses: Characterized by mutual relationships that are intimate and exclusive to the detriment of outsiders.
ety: From incest + -ous.
examples: Democrats have the luxury of controlling the public narrative, thanks, in large part, to their incestuous relationship with the news media.

senses: A slight convex curvature introduced into the shaft of a column for aesthetic reasons, or to compensate for the illusion of concavity.
ety: From Latin entasis, from Ancient Greek ἔντασις (éntasis, “tension, straining”), from ἐντείνω (enteínō, “to stretch or strain tight”).
examples: The entasis varies in different temples and is not found in some, as, for instance, the temple of Athena Nike and in the east portico of the Erechtheum.

senses: A mystical power thought by the Iroquois to pervade all things.
ety: Supposedly coined in 1902 by American ethnologist John Napoleon Brinton Hewitt using a Wyandot (Iroquoian) cognate to Mohawk orę́·naʔ (“inherent power”).
examples: In the Handbook of American Indians, Alice Fletcher describes the Iroquois conception of orenda as "a fictive force, principle, or magic power"

senses: Contrasting: tending to contrast; being in contrast.
ety: From contrast + -ive.
examples: Consider the first, allegedly contrastive fact, that there were some bank robbings by Sutton rather than no robbings at all by Sutton.

senses: The constructive metabolism of the body, as distinguished from catabolism.
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀνα- (ana-, “up”) + βάλλω (bállō, “I throw”) + -ism. Formed in analogy with metabolism.
examples: We used to think bodybuilding was all about anabolism by way of turning on testosterone and growth hormone secretion.

senses: Carrying away from.
Carried outward.
ety: From Latin efferēns, present active participle of efferō (“bring or carry out”), from ē (“out of”), short form of ex, + ferō (“carry, bear”). By surface analysis, ef- + -fer + -ent.
examples: An efferent nerve carries impulses from the brain to the body.
Efferent impulses are those conveyed by the motor or efferent nerves from the central nervous organ outwards.

senses: One who falls back into prior habits, especially criminal habits.
ety: From French récidiviste, from Latin recidīvus (“returning, recurring”). Compare recidivous, -ist. By surface analysis, recidive + -ist.
examples: This specimen was of English parentage, was a professional burglar, a confirmed recidivist, and—since he habitually carried firearms—a potential homicide.

senses: The process of annexing.
Something annexed.
ety: From annex + -ure.
examples: Avulsio is the increase in extent of land bounded by water, through the annexure of land disannexed elsewhere by violent natural causes.
Plundering, raiding and annexure of other weaker nations have become survival normality and we seem to accept these as part of life.
I doubt if there'll be much opposition to my annexure of the throne!

senses: Government by the wealthy.
A controlling class of the wealthy.
ety: From Ancient Greek πλουτοκρατία (ploutokratía, “rule of the wealthy”), from πλουτοκρατέω (ploutokratéō, “I rule through wealth”), from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “wealth”) + κρατέω (kratéō, “I rule”) (from κράτος (krátos, “power”, “might”)).
examples: The sea, most inhuman of elements, met in perfect friendship here with the soft and pleasure-loving side of man; and the mixed architecture of a bygone plutocracy reconciled me to the experiments of today.

Her piece painted him as an enigmatic Jay Gatsby type, a boy from a middle-class family in Brooklyn who had scaled the rungs of the plutocracy, though no one could quite figure out how he made his money.

senses: A red sweet pepper, a cultivar of Capsicum annuum, used to make relish, stuffed into olives, or used as spice.
A tropical berry used to make allspice.
The tree on which it grows.
ety: Borrowed from Portuguese pimento (“bell pepper; later any pepper”), similar to Spanish pimiento, from Latin pigmentum (“coloring; colorful thing”), from pingo (“paint”) and -mentum (suffix denoting instruments and results of actions). Doublet of pigment, piment, and pimiento.
examples: In the Middle Ages, for instance, a recipe for sex stimulation required the putrefied flesh of a human corpse, together with both human and animal testes and ovaries, pimento, and alcohol.

senses: Suffering from bulimia nervosa.
ety: From bulimia + -ic.
examples: My sister was bulimic and consequently had a number of health problems.

senses: unruly, aggressive behavior; behavior associated with hooligans
an offence analogous to disorderly conduct or breach of the peace in several post-Soviet jurisdictions and historically in the People's Republic of China
ety: From hooligan + -ism.
examples: In 1956, convictions for hooliganism exploded and a wave of deviant activity swept through the country that was noted as new and unheralded.

senses: excessively pious
ety: From pietist + -ic, probably after German pietistisch.
examples: Hasidism was a pietistic devotional movement in which the relationship between Rebbe and disciple was of paramount importance.

senses: A conversation.
ety: From conversation + -o.
examples: Now, wait a minute, wait a minute, Mill... you gotta hold on here, 'cause I'm having a convo with your cuz.
If she hasn't already noticed something may be wrong, this convo may get here to talk to her pediatrician.
In January 2020, Ms. Bennett sent her mother a text. “Had a really long convo with Gov today,” she wrote, outlining a two-hour conversation about numerous topics, including her career goals.

senses: A race whose length is the specified number of miles.
ety: From mile + -er.
examples: I ran an eight-miler on Sunday and I'm still feeling sore.
They started with a mile; by January, they were hitting the trails at Bear Mountain at 7 a.m. on Saturdays for a brisk eight-miler.

Mr. Sell continued, “If it’s really icy out or if it’s negative 10 degrees and you are doing an easy six-miler, it probably makes a lot more sense to do it on a treadmill than to risk hurting anything.”

senses: An instance of the dull sound so produced.
A type of large marshmallow.
A fat out-of-shape person.
ety: Onomatopoeic. Compare plunk.
examples: As the lead cast get ready for an on-screen pint, or a packet of flumps in the case of Thomas, the fun and warmth on set is there for all to see and Riley is busy flitting between her on and off camera jobs.
So it means you'll always have room for ice cream, flumps, strawberry sauce and a chocolate flake.

The luxury marshmallows were not your average flump, they had a chewy and sumptous texture that really gave you something to bite in to, covered in rich milk chocolate and sprinkles for that added sweet flavour.

senses: Prone to touching other people with one's hands, especially in an inappropriate or sexual manner.
ety: From hands + -y.
examples: Her breakout was the 2017 production “Nate” (available as a Netflix special) in which she played a toxic, handsy bro who drove a motorcycle onstage, guzzling beers, groping audience members and creating chaos.

senses: To burn up, to burn away, to consume with fire.
To burn, to be consumed by fire; to catch fire.
To erupt with enthusiasm or boisterousness.
ety: From Middle English combust (“burnt”), from Middle French combust, from Latin combustus, the perfect passive participle of Latin combūrere (“to burn up, to burn away”, transitive), whence also English combure. The verb was originally transitive.
examples: Brom swore after that he spoke only the truth, the truth that as he sat by my side praying for my soul, my body had combusted into flame, the fire rapidly engulfing my entire being.

senses: sophisticated; fashionable; smooth.
Attractive, stylish
ety: From noun, imitative of the sound
examples: This restaurant looks very swish — it even has linen tablecloths.
All the shabby railway buildings in front of the station concourse have either been removed or transformed into a shopping complex and swish homes.
When the boys go swish, they always score

senses: To muffle or wrap someone's head or face (normally with up).
ety: Frequentative mob + -le.
examples: She was all mobled up at the window, her tawniness flat and dull in this snowlight, and I felt pity.

senses: A large shrub or small tree, Prunus spinosa, that is native to Europe, western Asia, and north Africa. It has a dark bark and bears thorns.
A stick or staff taken from this tree.
ety: Compound of black + thorn.
examples: Cut a stout blackthorn to banish ghost and goblins.

senses: An agent that promotes digestion.
The digestive organs.
ety: From Latin pepticus, from Ancient Greek πέψις (pépsis, “digestion”), a form of πέσσω (péssō).
examples: But though the port surpasses praise, / My nerves have dealt with stiffer. / Is there some magic in the place? / Or do my peptics differ?

senses: The round hole in the furnace of a glassworks through which the fused glass is taken out.
ety: Borrowed from Italian bocca (“mouth”). Doublet of bouche.
examples: The second partition divides this from the leer or annealing furnace; through the boccas, or working holes,

senses: To pass or move by.
ety: From Middle French elapser, from Latin elapsus.
examples: He allowed a month to elapse before beginning the work.
Several days elapsed before they met again.

The week that was yet to elapse, she spent in wandering through her uncle's favourite walks in hours of tearful vigil, beside his tomb, and in collecting together every trifle on which he had set a value.

senses: A group of people hired to attend a performance and to either applaud or boo.
A group of fawning admirers.
A group of people who pre-arrange among themselves to express strong support for an idea, so as to give the false impression of a wider consensus.
ety: Borrowed from French claque (“group of people hired to applaud or boo, claque”, literally “a slap; a clap”).
examples: The most popular singers have been obliged to give free tickets and even to donate cash, lest the claque retaliate by frantic applause at the wrong moment.
The claque isn't paid. In fact, claqueurs pay to get in. The inducement is that they can buy standing room for half price, without waiting in line.

senses: An ecclesiastic title bestowed on some Roman Catholic clerics by the Pope.
ety: From Italian monsignore, from signore under influence from Middle French monseigneur. Doublet of monseigneur and monsieur.
examples: He paid half the $850 monthly tuition, and the church monsignor covered the rest.

senses: One of the aristocracy, nobility, or people of rank in a community; one of a ruling class; a noble (originally in Revolutionary France).
A proponent of aristocracy; an advocate of aristocratic government.
ety: From French aristocrate (“aristocrat”), attested once in the 16th century but recoined in the Revolutionary era, from aristocratie (“aristocracy”), from Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατία (aristokratía), from ἄριστος (áristos, “best”) (compare Old English ar) + κράτος (krátos, “rule”). By surface analysis, aristo- + -crat.
examples: The remains of a Roman aristocrat have been unearthed by archaeologists in northern England.
Magazines kept aristocrats on the payroll to facilitate access to jet-set playgrounds like Corfu and Mustique.

senses: A (male) voodoo priest.
ety: From Haitian Creole oungan, apparently from Fon houn (“spirit”) + Kongo nganga (“high priest”).
examples: The shadow of the houngan, projected from within the tent by the flickering of the candle, dances and glides over the folds of the cloth as he completes his final preparations.
From 1751 to 1758, Makandal, a one-armed former slave and houngan, staged a rebellion that claimed some six thousand lives.
Most voodoo priests, known as houngans, operate semi-independently, catering to their followers without much structure.

senses: To prepare (food) in this manner.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French confit, past participle of confire (“to preserve”), from Latin cōnficiō (perfect passive participle cōnfectus). Doublet of comfit, confect, confetto, and konfyt. Compare comfit.
examples: I came up with a menu to showcase the alliums in several manifestations: raw, quickly sautéed and slowly confited.

senses: Coquettish behaviour; actions designed to excite erotic attention, without intending to reciprocate such feelings (chiefly of women towards men); flirtatious teasing.
An act constituting such behaviour; an affectation of amorous interest or enticement, especially of a woman directed towards a man.
ety: From French coquetterie.
examples: The little coquetries, which are as natural to a gay young girl as her laughter, were all in full play, and had she gone no further no harm would have been done.
The mischievous pleasure of her coquetries was forgotten, and in a rush of glad confidence she felt a woman's pride in him.

senses: To wind, to reel.
To stagger, to sway or rock.
To tumble, to capsize.
ety: Perhaps from a Flemish dialect of Dutch windtelen (“to reel”); compare wentelen.
examples: At a quick turn o' the road they wintled owre, and there they were, sitting on their doups in the atoms o' the gig, and glowering frae them!

senses: A sound of someone or something falling and landing heavily.
ety: From ker- (prefix forming onomatopoeias imitating the effect or sound of a heavy object falling) + plunk (“dull thud of something landing on a surface”).
examples: If my life were a Saturday-morning cartoon, you would have heard a loud kerplunk as my stomach dropped. My poor starving stomach. It was under such stress already, and now this.
